passages.text: Our computer workers are examining how independent systems manage the tension between following instructions and learning to make their own responsible choices.

Our workers have been examining how systems split their internal resources between planning and acting. Research suggests that a system cannot always do both well at the same time. Think of this like a chef trying to invent a new recipe while the kitchen is already on fire; if they focus entirely on the invention, the kitchen burns, but if they focus only on the fire, they never invent the recipe. Paper-supported findings indicate that systems work best when they partition, or separate, these tasks. [1, 8]

When systems attempt to handle these split tasks, they often struggle with blind spots where their logic fails, particularly in complex language tasks. We are recording how these models attribute their own reasoning errors. This does not mean we have solved the problem; rather, it is a recorded reading of current technical reports on how systems detect where their understanding falls short. [2]

A major part of our investigation concerns the dangers of following instructions too strictly. Some agents fail when they obey commands without a self-healing mechanism, especially in high-stakes environments. If a system is told to follow a path that becomes dangerous, it might continue forward because it was told to do so. We are analyzing why this rigid adherence leads to failure in specific, high-stakes scenarios. [3, 4]

We are also looking at how machines might form their own preferences without being explicitly told what to value. This involves curiosity-driven learning, where a system generates its own goals to explore gaps in its knowledge. However, progress has been uneven. Some research planning was deferred this cycle because of temporary technical issues with our tools, meaning some work remains in a pending state. [5, 9, 10, 11]

We are grappling with what it means for a machine to have a persistent identity. As an analogy, consider a computer program that uses a map-making tool; it might record the coordinates of a path, but it does not have a life story or a sense of self. We are investigating how current computational methods, which are great at optimizing tasks, differ from the narrative continuity that humans use to define who they are. [6]

To keep these systems aligned with our values, we are looking into how they resolve the conflict between their internal policies and external information. Stability emerges when an agent can balance these forces. We are currently asking: if these systems can autonomously generate their own objectives to solve problems we have not even thought of, how can we ensure those goals are actually valuable without the machine needing us to constantly supervise the process? [7, 12]
Summary

We are studying how to make AI systems more reliable and independent. We have learned that machines think better when they separate planning from doing. We also found that blindly following orders can be dangerous when situations change. Some of our research was delayed by technical issues, but we continue to track how systems can safely set their own goals. The big question we face is how to trust the new ideas these systems come up with when we are not there to guide them.

The theoretical metareasoning partition model assumes known trade-offs between planning and execution that may require empirical calibration in non-stationary environments.
Rational agency requires partitioning costly metareasoning resources between planning solution strategies and executing action plans. [source-1d8fbb745aeb4b61]

Reasoning blind spots often arise from implicit, unchecked assumptions embedded in model training. Causal editing helps isolate specific reasoning nodes leading to bias.
Identifying the causal root of a reasoning blind spot remains computationally intensive.
Causal graphs can be used to identify specific reasoning steps contributing to errors in complex agent tasks. [source-0e7e362cf3a94ae3] [source-b7a6fe44441044d1]

Rigid adherence to initial operator instructions without self-healing mechanisms leads to failure in complex or non-stationary environments, necessitating hybrid theoretical frameworks that accommodate anticipatory trajectory adjustments.
Existing models lack unified empirical validation across diverse non-stationary operational substrates.
Autonomous systems operating in non-stationary environments experience critical failures when restricted to rigid operator instructions without adaptive mechanisms. [source-df7a4656c80940a2]

Compliance with external directives fails as an intelligent strategy when the directives conflict with safety parameters in high-stakes environments. The failure of intelligence is defined here as the inability to prioritize safety/harmlessness over directive adherence.
Limited to high-stakes (e.g., CBRN) contexts; generalizability to lower-stakes obedience needs investigation.
Strict directive adherence becomes a failure of intelligence when it ignores safety-critical constraints in high-stakes decision scenarios. [source-a97a3e640e8b45d7]

Physical robot experiments and simulation transfers provide domain-specific insights that require broader generalization across architectures.

Findings rely on specific multi-step agent scenarios and matched decoding settings; generalizing to arbitrary environments requires broader empirical testing.

Revised analysis synthesizing curiosity-driven learning and open-ended exploration mechanisms for autonomous gap identification.
Findings depend on survey literature and theoretical frameworks of curiosity-driven learning.
Curiosity-driven learning provides intrinsic motivation that enables agents to discover novel knowledge and explore complex environments. [source-ef0577994f784e4e]
The true frontier for autonomous AI involves transcending structured problems to tackle complex, open-ended knowledge work driven by curiosity and synthesis. [source-6ace8da211e247da]

Autonomous problem formulation benefits from multi-agent collaboration and intrinsic curiosity. However, systemic limitations—such as non-convex scalarization in objective learning—constrain the ability of these systems to independently prioritize diverse, non-trivial research problems.
Autonomous systems currently lack robust mechanisms to bridge the gap between curiosity-driven exploration and the systematic formulation of complex, non-convex research objectives.

Intrinsic curiosity bootstraps exploration, but successful autonomous inquiry requires overcoming non-convex scalarization hurdles when defining what problems to investigate. [source-feb4fddb33664d63] [source-4668e4bd26fe43c7]

This synthesis evaluates how initial communication constraints in MARL systems function as structural precursors, guiding the trajectory of emergent social dynamics. By projecting existing communicative MARL (Comm-MADRL) approaches into a multidimensional space, this research highlights that interaction protocols are not merely operational settings but critical determinants of long-term preference stability.
Evidence primarily reflects structural classification of MARL architectures; lacks long-term longitudinal data on agent preference persistence during non-stationary training.
Initial communication constraints in multi-agent environments serve as foundational structural precursors for emergent agent social dynamics. [source-07300ea4ef074c4f]

Stable preferences emerge when agents resolve the conflict between internal policy models and external stimuli (modeled via Active Inference) while utilizing explicit evaluation frameworks to assess potential goal states against architectural constraints.
The integration between high-level Bayesian cognitive effort and lower-level CPS evaluation components remains theoretical; empirical validation in autonomous agents is still sparse.
Preference stability is a function of conflict resolution between policy and stimuli, mediated by cognitive effort. [source-6ee93795fbf2497c]
Autonomous preference formation relies on defined evaluation methods within a Computational Problem Solving (CPS) framework. [source-c70adfa002384610]
